summary:
This is the opening page of **chapter 12, Object detection**. The "This chapter covers" box lists four topics:

- understanding the object detection problem,
- two-stage and single-stage object detectors,
- training a simple single-stage detector from scratch,
- using a pretrained object detector.

The opening paragraph defines the task: object detection is "all about drawing boxes (called *bounding boxes*) around objects of interest in a picture" (see Figure 12.1, printed on p.354). Detection tells you **which** objects are present and **where** they are. Three common applications follow:

- **Counting**: how many instances of an object are in an image;
- **Tracking**: following how objects move in a scene by running detection on every frame of a movie;
- **Cropping**: locating the region containing an object of interest so that a higher-resolution patch can be sent to a classifier or an Optical Character Recognition (OCR) model.

How to use this page: treat it as a map. According to the chapter outline, section 12.1 (p.354) contrasts two-stage R-CNN detectors with single-stage detectors, 12.2 (p.356) trains a YOLO model from scratch on COCO, and 12.3 (p.370) uses a pretrained RetinaNet. The page connects directly to chapter 11: the box prompts used with SAM on p.351-352 are exactly the kind of bounding box a detector outputs, and p.354 will argue that segmentation is a strict superset of detection but much costlier to run and to label.

paragraphs.excerpt: Object detection is all about drawing boxes (called bounding boxes) around
paragraphs.what_it_says: Object detection draws bounding boxes around objects of interest, telling you which objects are in a picture and where; it introduces a list of common applications.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A detector outputs, per object, a box (location and extent) and a class label. Compared with classification (one label per image) it adds location; compared with segmentation it gives only a rectangle rather than exact pixels.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This defines the output format the entire chapter builds toward, and it explains why detection is useful even though segmentation contains more information.

terminology.meaning: Axis-aligned rectangle enclosing an object, e.g. given by two corners as for SAM's box prompt (p.351).
Locating and labelling every object of interest in an image with a bounding box.

p.354: Figure 12.1 and the comparison with segmentation.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Detection can locate a region of interest so a higher-resolution crop can be passed to a classifier or OCR model. (Counting and tracking are the two shorter bullets above it.)
paragraphs.what_it_means: Detection often acts as the first stage of a pipeline: find the object cheaply at low resolution, then run a specialised model on just that patch at full resolution.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows detection as a building block, not only an end task; the same idea underlies two-stage detectors discussed in 12.1.

terminology.meaning: Optical Character Recognition: reading text from images.

connections: p.354: two-stage R-CNN detectors first propose regions, then classify them.

concepts.name: Object detection
concepts.definition: The task of drawing bounding boxes around objects of interest in an image (and labelling them).
concepts.intuition: Classification says 'there is a cat'; detection says 'there is a cat here'.
concepts.technical: Outputs a variable-length set of (box, class, score) triples per image.
concepts.significance: Enables counting, tracking and cropping applications.
concepts.example: Counting the fruit in the chapter 11 test image.
concepts.misconception: Detection does not give exact object outlines; that is segmentation.

concepts.name: Bounding box
concepts.definition: Rectangle around an object of interest.
concepts.intuition: The tightest frame around the object.
concepts.technical: Encoded by two corners (x0, y0, x1, y1) or by a corner/center plus width and height.
concepts.significance: The output unit of object detection.
concepts.misconception: A box is not a mask; background pixels inside the box are included.

misconceptions.claim: Object detection and image segmentation give the same information.
misconceptions.correction: Detection gives boxes; segmentation gives pixel masks. Segmentation is a superset but costs more to run and label (p.354).

takeaways: Object detection draws bounding boxes around objects: what and where.
Applications: counting, tracking (per-frame detection), cropping for downstream classifiers/OCR.
The chapter covers two-stage vs. single-stage detectors, a YOLO model from scratch, and a pretrained RetinaNet.

questions.question: What does object detection tell you that image classification does not?
questions.answer: Where the objects are (their bounding boxes), not only which objects are present.
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph says detection lets you know which objects are in a picture and where they are.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the applications listed on the page?
questions.explanation: The page lists counting, tracking and cropping. Denoising is an image-restoration task, not mentioned.

questions.question: How is tracking implemented according to the page?
questions.answer: By running object detection on every frame of a video and following how the detected objects move.
questions.explanation: The tracking bullet describes per-frame detection.

questions.question: Why would you crop a detected object and send a higher-resolution patch to a classifier or OCR model?
questions.answer: The detector can work on a downscaled whole image, while the specialised model gets the fine detail it needs only for the relevant region.
questions.explanation: The cropping bullet describes this pipeline; the efficiency reasoning is an explanation beyond the page's wording.

questions.question: Can you name the two families of detectors the chapter will compare, and which kind you will train from scratch?
questions.answer: Two-stage and single-stage detectors; a simple single-stage detector (YOLO) is trained from scratch.
